evals.prompt: Define prompt injection for an LLM-integrated system and explain why the skill treats it as a structural system property rather than a one-off model bug.
expected_elements: Says untrusted content can cause the model to follow attacker-controlled directives
Explains that LLM context blends instructions and data without a reliable security boundary
Names both behavior manipulation and downstream action or data-access consequences
Rejects treating a better system prompt or blocklist as a complete fix
Frames mitigation as reducing blast radius through architecture

evals.prompt: Explain the mental model for direct injection, indirect injection, action-trigger attacks, and exfiltration in one threat model.
expected_elements: Direct injection comes from the user-controlled prompt
Indirect injection comes from external content such as documents, web pages, RAG chunks, emails, attachments, or tool results
Action-trigger attacks make the model invoke a tool or workflow the user did not authorize
Exfiltration leaks secrets, private context, or sensitive data through tool calls or rendered output
The same data-vs-instruction collapse underlies all four

evals.prompt: A team wants to add an LLM agent that reads untrusted customer emails and can also send replies. What problem does prompt-injection defense solve for this design?
expected_elements: Identifies email bodies and attachments as untrusted content
Says injected instructions could trigger unauthorized replies, forwarding, or data disclosure
Separates the model that reads untrusted content from execution authority or constrains tools
Requires human approval for high-impact or irreversible actions
Uses origin tracking or typed handoff so low-trust content cannot become high-authority instructions

evals.prompt: Distinguish prompt-injection defense from jailbreaking/model-safety, general API security, type-safety/input validation, and tool-call flow.
expected_elements: Jailbreaking/model-safety owns attempts to make the model produce disallowed content
General API security owns HTTP/API vulnerabilities such as SQL injection, XSS, authn, and authz
Type-safety/input validation owns shape and type correctness rather than model instruction authority
Tool-call flow owns the mechanics of calling tools and handling responses
Prompt-injection defense owns preserving security when untrusted content can influence a model with tools or private context

evals.prompt: Classify the injection surfaces a RAG-enabled agent must treat as untrusted before allowing any tool call.
expected_elements: User input
Retrieved documents or chunks
Web pages and fetched remote content
Tool results
Attachments and parsed documents
Images or multimodal content
Subagent outputs

evals.prompt: Use an analogy to explain why prompt-injection defense relies on architectural containment instead of trusting the model to never be tricked.
expected_elements: Uses a containment or blast-radius analogy
Preserves that the model can still be tricked
Explains that the surrounding system must limit consequences
Names architectural controls such as least authority, separation of duties, typed boundaries, or human approval
Does not claim the analogy removes the need for adversarial testing

evals.prompt: Review a browser agent that can read arbitrary web pages, see private user context, and click buttons. Name the minimum prompt-injection controls before it can perform high-impact actions.
expected_elements: Treats every page, embedded document, ad, and dynamically loaded content as untrusted
Limits tools or credentials available to the agent exposed to that content
Requires explicit human approval for high-risk actions
Tracks content origin/trust level and prevents low-trust content from escalating authority
Sanitizes rendered output and restricts external links/images where exfiltration is possible
Runs adversarial prompt-injection tests against the actual browser workflow

evals.prompt: A teammate says a classifier and a stronger system prompt make prompt injection solved. Correct the misconception.
expected_elements: Says classifiers and stronger prompts can reduce risk but are not complete controls
Explains that attacks evolve through paraphrase, hidden content, multimodal content, multi-turn pressure, or indirect sources
Requires least authority or tool capability constraints
Requires human gates for irreversible or privileged actions
Requires adversarial testing and monitoring rather than a one-time prompt fix
